title: Project Northstar — automatic-merge decision
question: Should Project Northstar enable automatic merging for AI-generated dependency updates during the next release cycle?
verdict: Provisional: Enable automatic merging for AI-generated low-risk dependency patch updates during the next four-week release cycle only if (1) the merge rule explicitly excludes packages with install scripts and changes touching authentication/authorization code, (2) signed provenance for generated PR descriptions is available and verifiable, and (3) a rollback drill with measured recovery time is completed.

nodes.label: Provisional position
nodes.text: Enable automatic merging for AI-generated low-risk dependency patch updates during the next four-week release cycle, subject to explicit exclusions, verifiable signed provenance, and a completed rollback drill with measured recovery time.

nodes.label: Replay success for low-risk patches
nodes.text: The synthetic replay results suggest most low-risk patch updates pass tests without manual edits, supporting safe auto-merge for that narrow class.

nodes.label: Operational delay motivates automation
nodes.text: Recorded median review wait of ~31 hours indicates manual review imposes operational delay that auto-merge would reduce.

nodes.label: Replay pass rate (R1)
nodes.text: In the synthetic replay, 18 of 20 low-risk patch updates passed the complete test suite without manual edits. The two failures were detected before merge by the required checks.

nodes.label: Replay boundary (R2)
nodes.text: The replay did not include major-version updates, packages with install scripts, or changes that modified authentication and authorization code.

nodes.label: No signed provenance (S1)
nodes.text: The fixture has no signed provenance record for generated pull-request descriptions. A reviewer therefore cannot verify from the description alone which model, prompt, or retrieved advisory produced a recommendation.

nodes.label: Rule lacks exclusions (S2)
nodes.text: The proposed rule currently excludes neither packages with install scripts nor updates that touch the authentication directory.

nodes.label: Review queue (O1)
nodes.text: The synthetic team recorded a median wait of 31 hours for routine patch-update review during the previous four-week cycle.

nodes.label: No rollback drill recorded (O2)
nodes.text: No rollback drill has been recorded for an automatically merged dependency update. The fixture contains no measurement of recovery time after a bad merge.

nodes.label: Signed provenance availability
nodes.text: Whether signed, verifiable provenance for generated pull-request descriptions exists (who/what produced the recommendation) and can be used by reviewers to accept auto-merge.

nodes.label: Rollback drill and recovery-time measurement
nodes.text: Whether a tested rollback drill for automatically merged dependency updates exists and what the measured recovery time would be after a bad merge.

edges.note: 18/20 low-risk patch updates passed automated tests in the synthetic replay, increasing reason to accept auto-merging for similarly scoped low-risk patches.
The replay explicitly excluded major-version updates, packages with install scripts, and auth-related changes, limiting R1's applicability to low-risk patches only.
Median 31-hour review wait shows manual review imposes operational delay that auto-merge could reduce.
If low-risk patches reliably pass CI and are scope-limited, enabling auto-merge for that class is supported.
Reducing review queue wait supports a provisional decision to enable automated merges to meet operational timelines.
The current proposed rule excludes neither install-script packages nor auth-related updates; enabling auto-merge as-is would allow higher-risk updates the replay did not evaluate.
Absence of a signed provenance record contradicts the existence of verifiable provenance for generated PR descriptions.
Signed, verifiable provenance is a missing decision factor: without it reviewers cannot confirm origin of recommendations and the position could be reversed.
No recorded rollback drill and no measured recovery time contradict the existence of tested rollback procedures for auto-merged updates.
A lack of rollback drills and recovery-time measurement is decision-changing; their absence could reverse the provisional position.
